papers.title: Limits and Constants of OpenAI's Claimed ETH Refutation
papers.abstract: A recent OpenAI preprint claims a deterministic algorithm that counts the satisfying assignments of a $k$-CNF formula in time $2^{O_k(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}$, and $2^{O(n/\sqrt{\log n})}$ at bounded clause density, which would refute the Exponential Time Hypothesis. The headline bound is proved by tensor contraction; the body develops an interpolation algorithm with the weaker exponent $n(\log\log n)^2/\sqrt{\log n}$. This note does four things. First, it explains the interpolation algorithm in plain terms. Second, it asks how large $n$ must be for the bounds to bite. The preprint states no constants, so we treat the hidden constant $C$ as a parameter: the general bound beats the $2^n$ of brute force only beyond $n\approx 10^{32}$ for $C=2$, $10^{126}$ for $C=3$ and $10^{3517}$ for $C=10$. We then extract the constants from the tensor-contraction proof: for every input with $m$ clauses at bounded density, the running time it certifies stays above $2^n$ unless $\log_2(n+m)>10^9$, and on random 3-CNF at the satisfiability threshold unless $\log_2 n>5\times10^{11}$. So the bounds are subexponential as $n\to\infty$, but the proof certifies no speed-up over brute force for any input of bounded density that could ever be written down. Third, for the clause-product form of the interpolation algorithm we prove limits in a cost model matching the preprint's evaluation. By a short algebraic lemma, polynomial cost needs components of $O(\log^3 n)$ variables with per-point evaluation, or primal treewidth $O(\log^2 n)$ with dynamic programming over the groups. So the scheme costs $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\mathrm{tw}})}$ at treewidth $\mathrm{tw}$, $2^{\Omega(\sqrt n)}$ with high probability on random 3-CNF above clause density 3, and $2^{\Omega(n^{1/3})}$ even on trivially countable path formulas. We explain why the preprint's sharper routes escape these limits. Fourth, we report experiments.

papers.title: A Numerical Refinement of an Exact Discrete Fourier Transform Bound
papers.abstract: We refine the numerical bounds in Kartal's instantiation of Sussman's exact discrete Fourier transform construction. For every integer n >= 1, the resulting algorithm computes the length-n transform with work O(n (log n)^(1 - delta)), where delta = 0.0030201659. The bound holds in an exact complex-arithmetic RAM model with a supplied canonical root of unity. This final exponent saving exceeds the earlier certified parameter C_0 = 0.00302016 by 5.9 x 10^(-9). We retain the underlying circuit, tighten rational bounds for sums of powers of its block and target ranks, and increase the fixed tensor power from 7760 to 11640. These bounds establish the inequalities for Sussman's recursion at the intermediate certificate parameter C = 0.00302016595. The gap C - delta absorbs the overhead of recursion and Fourier reduction. The resulting transform theorem is proved in Lean and checked against the reference problem statement.

papers.title: A Decomposition Theorem and a Simple Algorithm for Contraction Fixed Points
papers.abstract: We prove a decomposition theorem for the problem of computing an approximate fixed point of a contraction map $f\colon [0,1]^k \to [0,1]^k$ under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm. After a preliminary version of the decomposition theorem appeared on arXiv [CLY26], Feodorov and Haslebacher [FH26] gave a striking application of the theorem, showing that it can be used to convert any $\operatorname{poly}(k,\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm with running time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(k)}$ into an algorithm with running time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(\sqrt{k})}$. They instantiated this framework with an $O(k^2\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm with the desired running time, thereby obtaining the first subexponential-time algorithm for contraction fixed points under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm and, via well-known reductions, the first deterministic subexponential-time algorithm for simple stochastic games and mean-payoff games. In addition to the decomposition theorem, as our second main result in this paper, we show that the $O(k\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm of [CLY25] can be implemented in time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(k)}$; our algorithm may be viewed as conceptually simpler compared to the algorithm of [FH26]. A key observation here is that the function constructed in [CLY25], whose fixed points are used as the next query points, turns out to be nonexpansive under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm, so the brute-force procedure can be replaced by known algorithms for contraction fixed points.

papers.title: Fine-Grained Complexity Across the Computational Phase Transition
papers.abstract: How does a computational problem transition from easy to hard? In the hard-core model, approximate counting and sampling are polynomial-time tractable up to tree uniqueness, but worst-case intractable at any constant relative distance above it unless $\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{RP}$. We quantify the transition from polynomial to exponential mixing for classical Glauber dynamics. On $n$-vertex graphs of maximum degree $d\ge3$, at fugacity $\lambda=(1+\delta)\lambda_{\mathrm c}(d)$ with sufficiently small $\delta\ge0$ that may vanish with $n$, its worst-case mixing time has the form $\exp\{\Theta(n\delta^2/d)\}n^{1+\Theta(1)}$. The upper bound is degree-uniform, and the matching lower bound holds for every fixed $d$. Annealing gives approximate counting with the same running-time upper bound at fixed accuracy. For general sampling and counting algorithms, we establish a robust fine-grained reduction from SAT without assuming a lower bound on SAT's running time. For any fixed $d\ge3$ and $0<\gamma<1$, a sampling or approximate-counting algorithm running in $\exp\{O((n\delta^2/d)^{1-\gamma})\}\operatorname{poly}(n)$ time along any one suitable inverse-polynomial distance sequence $\delta=\delta(n)$, yields a randomized SAT algorithm running in $\exp\{\widetilde O(s^{1-\gamma})\}$ time on inputs of binary length $s$. This power-saving transfer identifies $n\delta^2/d$ as the analogue of SAT input length for hard-core sampling and counting at relative distance $\delta$ above criticality: beating the Glauber exponent by a fixed power through any sampling or counting method would yield a corresponding power improvement for SAT. At criticality, we establish $O(\sqrt{n/d})$ spectral independence, optimal in $n$ at fixed degree, and degree-uniform Glauber mixing in $\widetilde O(n(n/d)^{1+1/(d-2)})$ time, improving the previous $\widetilde O(n^{4+4/(d-2)})$ bound.

papers.title: Online Algorithms Cannot Find Isolated Perceptron Solutions
papers.abstract: The binary perceptron problem asks for a length-$n$ sign vector in the intersection of $\lfloor \alpha n\rfloor$-many independent random Gaussian half-spaces. A striking feature of this model is strong freezing: at every constraint density $\alpha > 0$, all but a vanishing fraction of solutions are isolated -- $\Omega(n)$-far from all others, in Hamming distance. Such solutions are believed to be algorithmically inaccessible. Nevertheless, efficient algorithms find solutions at some constraint densities $\alpha$. One possible resolution of this apparent contradiction is that the solution space also contains rare well-connected structures, and that algorithms succeed by locating them. Gong, Huang, Li and Sellke (FOCS 2026) proved this for stable algorithms, by showing that such algorithms cannot locate isolated solutions with probability more than $\approx 0.84$. In this work, we study online algorithms, which receive the columns of the constraint matrix one by one and sign each irrevocably upon arrival. This is a widely used class of algorithms in discrepancy minimization, and it includes the algorithm of Jo and Lee (2026), which has one of the best provable guarantees for the binary perceptron. We prove that at any constraint density, any online algorithm outputs an isolated solution with probability $o(1)$. Our proof is based on the observation that the signs an online algorithm has already fixed can be completed to at most one isolated solution, so a successful algorithm must choose the unique correct sign for each of the last few columns. Using the exchangeability of these columns, we show that such an algorithm must match a suffix-parallel baseline, which signs each of them as if it were the next column to arrive. We then use an anti-concentration argument to show that such a baseline rarely produces a unique completion.

papers.title: Compressed Oracle Duality: A simple framework for knowing what quantum adversaries know
papers.abstract: Given a quantum adversary that queries a random oracle, how do we characterize the information that they "know"? The Compressed Oracle method of Zhandry (CRYPTO 2019) is one method that records the queries that the adversary makes; this recording serves as a representation of the information that is learned. However, a significant limitation of the Compressed Oracle method is that it may continue to store information that the adversary has "forgotten." This issue is especially pertinent in the space-bounded setting, where the adversary may uncompute information to free up space, while the information may still reside in the compressed oracle. In this work, we present a simple and interpretable framework called "Compressed Oracle Duality," which extends the Compressed Oracle method for space-bounded algorithms. By applying an isometry to the memory of a quantum adversary, we obtain a pair of compressed oracles with identical marginal distributions and classical correlations which correspond to the knowledge the adversary retains. In fact, we show that the outcome of measuring the new compressed oracle database corresponds exactly to applying the pretty-good measurement on the adversary's memory. As an application of our framework for collision search, we give a simplified proof of the recent $T^2S = \Omega(N\log N)$ quantum time-space tradeoff for label-symmetric algorithms due to Magniez-Zur (arXiv:2609.10808); we also prove a stronger classical tradeoff of $TS=\Omega(N\log N)$ assuming label symmetry. The proofs under our framework do not require representation theory and instead bound the mutual information between the compressed oracle pairs. This highlights both how the label symmetry assumption bypasses known proof barriers as well as the challenges that remain in achieving unconditional quantum time-space tradeoffs.

papers.title: The Value of Steiner Hubs in Two-Hop Distance Labeling
papers.abstract: Two-hop distance labelings were introduced in 2002 by Cohen, Halperin, Kaplan, and Zwick with hubs of two kinds: vertices of the graph, or, in their Steiner variant, arbitrary objects carrying arbitrary real values. On no family is the value of that freedom known. We determine it on $\ell_1$ products of betweenness-free metrics, those with no point between two others, a class containing every Hamming graph. The freedom is worth nothing when the factors have at most three letters, while from four letters on the largest saving is polynomial in the size of the product, attained on products of positively weighted stars. The $d$-dimensional hypercube is the two-letter case, and labeling it takes $(5/2+o(1))^d$ entries even with arbitrary hubs, matching the vertex-hub optimum of Goldberg, Razenshteyn, and Savchenko. Every lower bound here comes from one semidefinite program on a single factor, whose value $\Lambda$ never exceeds the rate that vertex hubs already achieve on the Hamming graph; where $\Lambda$ meets that ceiling, the freedom is worth nothing, and the ceiling is met exactly up to three letters.

papers.title: The Movement Complexity of Sorting
papers.abstract: The complexity of sorting is usually measured by the number of comparisons. This measure ignores the movement of the read heads between comparisons, which is a real cost on many machines. We study this cost on its own. Keys lie on a $d$-dimensional grid, two heads move over the grid and compare the keys beneath them, and the only cost is the total movement of the heads. The algorithm plans its route in $r$ rounds and sees the outcomes of each round only after running it. For every $d$ and $r$ we determine the expected movement needed to sort $n$ keys: it is $n^{\beta}$ up to polylogarithmic factors, where $\beta=1+D^{r-1}/(D^{r}-(D-1)^{r})$ and $D=2d$, falling from $n^{2}$ at $r=1$ to $n^{1+1/(2d)}$ with unlimited rounds. Our algorithm makes every round move about the same amount, and a matching lower bound holds against every algorithm.

papers.title: How Much Can Approximate Equilibria Change the Social Cost of Selfish Routing?
papers.abstract: We study approximate Nash equilibria in nonatomic congestion games, with the goal of understanding how much the social cost can change when the equilibrium condition is relaxed. We consider $\epsilon$-approximate Nash equilibria ($\epsilon$-NE), in which each player uses a strategy whose cost is at most $1 + \epsilon$ times the minimum available cost. We compare the social costs of $\epsilon$-NE and exact Nash equilibria. This lets us quantify, for example, how much a navigation app can reduce total travel time when drivers tolerate routes slightly slower than the fastest available route. For degree-$d$ polynomial latencies in both general nonatomic congestion games and single-commodity routing games on series-parallel networks, we give tight lower and upper bounds on the relative change in social cost from an exact Nash equilibrium to any $\epsilon$-NE, with matching instances for every $\epsilon$. For small $\epsilon$, the largest possible relative reduction and increase in general congestion games are both $\Theta(\sqrt{d\epsilon})$, independently of the number of resources and populations. In contrast, on series-parallel networks of depth $h$, the largest possible relative reduction is $\Theta(h\epsilon)$, while the largest possible relative increase is known to be $\epsilon$. For the classes of games we study, these results give a tight and quantitative characterization of the possible changes in social cost and establish a separation between general and series-parallel networks.

papers.title: An $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ for Mixed Volumes
papers.abstract: We design the first fully polynomial-time randomized approximation scheme ($\mathsf{FPRAS}$) to estimate the mixed volume of $n$ arbitrary compact convex sets in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ specified by weak membership oracles. This disproves a longstanding conjecture of Gurvits (2009). $\textbf{AI Disclosure}$ The main ideas were generated entirely by GPT 6 Astra. The purpose of this paper is to provide a human-written exposition of the algorithm.

papers.title: Efficient Proper Agnostic Learning of Halfspaces
papers.abstract: We give a proper membership-query algorithm for agnostically learning halfspaces under the uniform distribution on $\{\pm1\}^n$. Given query access to an arbitrary function $f:\{\pm1\}^n \to \{\pm1\}$, our algorithm runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)+2^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}$ and outputs a halfspace with error at most $\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the error of the best-fitting halfspace for $f$. Previously, even with membership queries, the best known running time was $n^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}$, achieved by the sample-based algorithm of Kalai, Klivans, Mansour, and Servedio (FOCS 2005). Our algorithm is the first agnostic halfspace learner under the uniform distribution on $\{\pm1\}^n$ whose running time is polynomial in $n$ with an exponent independent of $\varepsilon$. Combining our algorithm with a boosting argument yields a proper agnostic learner using only random examples. It achieves the same $\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$ guarantee, with running time matching that of Kalai et al.\ up to an additive term depending only on $\varepsilon$. To our knowledge, this is the first sample-based proper agnostic learner in the Boolean setting with running time $2^{o(n)}$ for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$.

papers.title: Circuit Lower Bounds for Extended Gate Bases from Subexponential Counting
papers.abstract: We study circuit lower bounds for extended gate bases using exact CNF counting and an extension-ring form of the contraction theorem of OpenAI. The deterministic counting theorem of Claude (Anthropic) yields an $\mathsf{E}^{\mathsf{NP}}$ language requiring $\Omega(m\sqrt{\log m}/\log\log m)$ gates over unbounded AND/OR with binary XOR, infinitely often. Using that contraction theorem, a bounded binary base with a linear budget of arbitrary XOR and symmetric gates requires $\Omega(m\sqrt{\log m})$ gates infinitely often. These results extend the binary-gate lower bound of OpenAI. Signed long-clause selectors reduce the first counting problem to the difference of two ordinary 3-CNF counts. Affine characters and unit-separated interpolation give the second counting interface, with logarithmic cost per symmetric-gate arity. A quantitative local-reduction transfer accounts for auxiliary variables, branch counts, and integer recovery.

papers.title: Full-Rank Constructions of Explicit Lossless Expanders and Good Small-Set qLTCs
papers.abstract: We construct explicit two-sided lossless expanders whose binary adjacency matrices have full rank, and use them to obtain explicit asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes whose specified X- and Z-check matrices have full row rank and satisfy small-set soundness, or confinement, on a linear range. Our lossless expanders are a variant of those of Hsieh, Lubotzky, Mohanty, Reiner, and Zhang, with a free action of a finite 2-group. Under such an action, injectivity and surjectivity of the adjacency matrix are detected on a fixed-size matrix indexed by vertex orbits. Adding a sparse factor to the gadget at the middle vertices of a single type then enforces full rank, with a controlled loss in expansion. To obtain the 2-group action, we observe that reducing the generators of the Lubotzky-Phillips-Sarnak Ramanujan graphs modulo powers of 2, instead of modulo an odd prime, gives Ramanujan Cayley graphs on finite 2-groups. This construction may be of independent interest. Plugging two such expanders into the balanced product of Lin and Hsieh gives the quantum codes, since full rank of the input graphs is inherited by the check matrices. Our construction supplies the code family sought by Hong, Guo, and Lucas. Applying their analysis, within their framework and under their dynamical assumptions, gives quantum memories whose free-energy density is analytic at every positive temperature and whose guaranteed lifetime is $exp(\Omega(N))$ at sufficiently low fixed positive temperature, where N is the blocklength. This improves the previously guaranteed stretched-exponential timescale.

papers.title: Worst-Case to Average-Case Reductions for Basic Linear Algebra
papers.abstract: We study worst-case to average-case reductions for basic linear-algebraic problems over finite fields. A seminal work of Blum, Luby, and Rubinfeld established that any algorithm that successfully multiplies more than $75\%$ of matrix pairs over any finite field, implies an algorithm with essentially the same running time multiplying any pair of matrices. A sequence of follow-ups reduced the needed fraction of successful input pairs to any positive constant. Despite most of the other basic linear algebraic operations being computationally equivalent to matrix multiplication in the worst case, no such worst-case to average-case reductions were known for them. Recently, Vaikuntanathan and Zamir introduced a cryptographic primitive called trapdoor matrices and used them to prove such worst-case to average-case reductions for matrix inversion, solving a linear system, and computing the determinant, all conditioned on common cryptographic assumptions. Our main result is the first unconditional time-preserving worst-case to average-case reduction for matrix inversion. Any algorithm that correctly inverts any constant positive fraction of uniformly random invertible matrices implies a worst-case such algorithm. We also significantly strengthen the conditional reductions based on trapdoored matrices: We establish reductions for deciding invertibility and computing rank at the optimal success thresholds, and qualitatively improve the success threshold needed in the reduction for determinant computation---while previous reductions all required the success probability to be at least $1/2$, we show that any fixed positive average-case success probability suffices for exact worst-case determinant computation over infinitely many finite fields.

papers.title: A GPU Engine for Sparse Matrix-Vector Products on $k^2$-Tree-Compressed Graphs
papers.abstract: The $k^2$-tree is a compact representation of Boolean matrices: it stores the recursive hierarchy of their non-empty submatrices, with neither values nor coordinates, and serves rows and columns alike. Its traversal, however, locates the children of each node by rank queries, a chain of dependent irregular loads that leaves a GPU waiting on memory. We implement sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) on $k^2$-trees for the GPU. Since the traversal does not depend on the vector, the positions of the children are static: we descend the tree one level at a time and obtain them from a parallel prefix sum or from a sampled directory of about 0.1 bits per node. Descending in tiles bounds the temporary memory by the depth of the tree, so the device memory of a product is known before it runs. The same traversal computes right and left products, for one vector or a batch, over the plus-times, Boolean and tropical semirings. We evaluate the engine on an NVIDIA GB10 and an H100 with fourteen Wikidata, Software Heritage, web and social graphs of up to 1.2 billion edges, against cuSPARSE, a grammar-compressed GPU engine and a Boolean CSR. Our results show that the tree is 2.3-27x smaller than the CSR of cuSPARSE and that, with its last internal level cached, a product takes 0.7-2.4x the time of cuSPARSE on the right and 0.27-2.6x on the left. On a 1.2-billion-edge graph, a product needs 1.1 GB on the device, 9x less than cuSPARSE. The engine is memory bounded: the $k^2$-tree is the format of choice when device memory, not time, is the constraint.

papers.title: Get Permanent Results Faster by Counting Stars
papers.abstract: We show that $n \times n$ permanents can be computed with $O^*{(2-\varepsilon)^n}$ arithmetic operations over every commutative ring, for $\varepsilon = 10^{-40}$. This solves a problem stated in Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming. Our algorithm implements the classical Binet--Minc identity with dynamic programming and careful bookkeeping. It also gives algebraic branching programs of size $O^*{(2-\varepsilon)^n}$.

papers.title: Tight (Double) Exponential Bounds for Identification Problems: Locating-Dominating Set and Test Cover
papers.abstract: We investigate fine-grained algorithmic aspects for classical identification problems in graphs, namely LOCATING-DOMINATING SET, and in set systems, namely TEST COVER. In the first problem, an input is a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and an integer $k$, and the objective is to decide whether there is a subset $S$ of $k$ vertices such that any two distinct vertices not in $S$ are dominated by distinct subsets of $S$. In the second problem, an input is a set $U$ of items, a collection $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $U$ called tests, and an integer $k$, and the objective is to select a set $S$ of at most $k$ tests such that any two distinct items are contained in a distinct subset of tests of $S$. For our first result, we show that LOCATING-DOMINATING SET (respectively, TEST COVER) parameterized by the treewidth of the input graph (respectively, the incidence graph) does not admit an algorithm running in time $2^{2^{o(\textsf{tw})}} \cdot {\rm poly}(n)$ (respectively, $2^{2^{o(\textsf{tw})}} \cdot {\rm poly}(|U| + |\mathcal{F}|)$), unless the ETH fails. Next, we prove that, unless the ETH fails, LOCATING-DOMINATING SET does not admit an algorithm running in time $2^{o(k^2)} \cdot {\rm poly}(n)$, nor a polynomial-time kernelization algorithm that reduces the solution size and outputs a kernel with $2^{o(k)}$ vertices, and TEST COVER does not admit an algorithm running in time $2^{2^{o(k)}} \cdot {\rm poly}(|U| + |\mathcal{F}|)$ nor a kernel with $2^{2^{o(k)}}$ vertices. Again, we show that these lower bounds are tight by designing (kernelization) algorithms with matching running times.

papers.title: Theoretical Analysis of Byte-Pair Encoding
papers.abstract: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) is a widely used method for subword tokenization, with origins in grammar-based text compression. It is employed in a variety of language processing tasks such as machine translation or large language model (LLM) pretraining, to create a token dictionary of a prescribed size. Most evaluations of BPE to date are empirical, and the reasons for its good practical performance are not well understood. In this paper we focus on the optimization problem underlying BPE: finding a pair encoding that achieves optimal compression utility. We show that this problem is APX-complete, indicating that it is unlikely to admit a polynomial-time approximation scheme. This answers, in a stronger form, a question recently raised by Zouhar et al. On the positive side, we show that BPE approximates the compression utility of the optimal pair encoding to a worst-case factor between $1/3$ and $(1-e^{-2})/2 \approx 0.4324$. Our results aim to explain the ongoing success of BPE and are, to our knowledge, the first rigorous guarantees on its compression utility that hold for all inputs.

papers.title: Identification to Subclasses of Chordal Graphs
papers.abstract: An identification of two vertices \(u\) and \(v\) in a graph replaces them with a new vertex that is made adjacent to every vertex of \(N(u)\cup N(v)\setminus \{u,v\}\). We study the \(\mathcal{H}\)-Identification problem, which is to decide whether a given graph \(G\) can be transformed (``identified'') to a graph in \(\mathcal{H}\) by applying at most \(k\) vertex identifications. We determine the classical and parameterized complexity of this problem for various subclasses \(\mathcal{H}\) of chordal graphs, obtaining an almost complete picture for two parameters: \(k\) and \(n-k\). We also consider the Identification problem, which is to test, for two given graphs \(G\) and \(H\), whether \(G\) can be identified to \(H\). We determine the parameterized complexity of this problem when \(H\) is a graph from one of our testbed classes, taking the number of simplicial vertices of \(H\) as the parameter.

papers.title: Quantizing With Randomized Hadamard Transforms: Efficient Heuristic Now Proven
papers.abstract: Uniform random rotations (URRs) are a common preprocessing step in modern quantization approaches used for gradient compression, inference acceleration, KV-cache compression, model weight quantization, and approximate nearest-neighbor search in vector databases. In practice, URRs are often replaced by randomized Hadamard transforms (RHTs), which preserve orthogonality while admitting fast implementations. The remaining issue is the performance for worst-case inputs. With a URR, each coordinate is distributed as a shifted beta distribution, which converges to a Gaussian distribution in high dimensions. Generally, one RHT is not suitable in the worst case, as individual coordinates can be far from these distributions. We show that after composing two RHTs on any $d$-sized input vector, the marginal distribution of every fixed coordinate of the normalized rotated vector is within $O(d^{-1/2})$ of a standard Gaussian both in Kolmogorov distance and in $1$-Wasserstein distance. We then plug these bounds into the analyses of modern compression schemes, namely DRIVE and QUIC-FL, and show that two RHTs achieve performance that asymptotically matches URRs. However, while two RHTs suffice for scalar quantization, they may be insufficient for Vector Quantization (VQ), which depends on the joint distribution across fixed-size blocks of coordinates (as opposed to only marginal distribution convergence for single coordinates). We prove that a composition of three RHTs leads to decaying coordinate covariance. This ensures that any fixed, bounded, multi-dimensional VQ codebook optimized for URRs has the same expected error when using three RHTs, up to an additive term that vanishes with the dimension. Finally, because practical inputs are rarely adversarial, we propose a linear-time $O(d)$ check on the input's moments to dynamically adapt the number of RHTs used at runtime to improve performance.

papers.title: Exponential Quantum Advantage in Testing Fourier Dimensionality
papers.abstract: A boolean function $f$ has Fourier dimension $k$ if its strings with nonzero Fourier coefficients span a subspace of dimension $k$. We first consider the property testing task of determining whether a function has Fourier dimension at most $k$, or is $\epsilon$-far from being so. We show that there is an $O(k/\sqrt{\epsilon})$-query quantum property tester for this problem, which we show to be almost optimal. Combined with Gopalan \etal's classical lower bound of $\Omega(2^{k/2})$, this demonstrates an exponential quantum advantage for this task. We complement this result with a $\tilde{O}(2^{k/2}/\epsilon)$ classical tester, giving a quadratic improvement over the previous best tester, and essentially settling the classical query complexity. We then introduce and study the tolerant version of this problem. That is, determining whether a function is $\alpha\epsilon$-close to having Fourier dimension at most $k$, or is $\epsilon$-far from being so. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that this tolerant version of the problem is essentially just as hard as the standard version of the problem. That is, we show this problem has a $\tilde{O}(k/\epsilon)$ quantum tester, and a $\tilde{O}(2^{k/2}/\epsilon)$ classical tester.

papers.title: Lower Bounds for Parallel Diffusion Sampling
papers.abstract: Standard diffusion samplers generate samples through sequential evaluations of a learned score function, with each query depending on previous answers. Parallel samplers seek to accelerate this process by making multiple score queries simultaneously. We ask how many adaptive rounds are necessary when each round allows polynomially many queries. We establish the first polynomial lower bounds on the round complexity of diffusion sampling with approximate scores satisfying a mean-square accuracy guarantee. Specifically, we prove (1) a $\widetilde{\Omega}(d^{1/3})$-round lower bound for sampling smooth, near-isotropic Gaussian mixtures in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and (2) a tight $\Omega(d)$-round lower bound for uniform sampling from anisotropic axis-aligned boxes contained in the unit ball. Both bounds hold for arbitrary randomized algorithms making polynomially many queries per round at arbitrary locations and noise levels, with inverse-polynomial score error and constant total variation accuracy. Our near-isotropic construction follows the blockwise approach of earlier lower bounds for parallel matroid search and discrete sampling \cite{KUW85,AGR24}. We use independent coordinate blocks containing random codebooks with well-separated rates and construct approximate score oracles whose responses in each block depend on consistency tests in earlier blocks. Together, the rate separation and these tests ensure that each round reveals information about at most one additional block with high probability.

papers.title: Subset Sum via Partial Match
papers.abstract: We show that the subset sum problem can be solved in randomized time $O(2^{0.49999\overline{7}n})$, breaking the $2^{n/2}$ meet-in-the-middle barrier. Our approach builds on the representation technique framework of Randolph and W\k{e}grzycki (STOC 2026). We choose a representation for which testing the compatibility of pairs of partial solution vectors is exactly the partial match problem. To beat exponent $1/2$ for subset sum, it then suffices to give a nontrivial partial match algorithm in a certain parameter regime. We achieve this by designing a depth-2 linear circuit for the partial match matrix, which yields an efficient algorithm via the framework of Alman and Li (FOCS 2025).

papers.title: Undirected Multiple-Unicast Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
papers.abstract: In undirected multiple-unicast networks, where independent messages are sent between specified source--destination pairs, network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages, whereas fractional routing splits and forwards individual messages along paths without mixing them. Proposed in 2004 by Li and Li and independently by Harvey, Kleinberg, and Lehman, the multiple-unicast conjecture---a central conjecture in network coding with deep connections to computational complexity---asserts that network coding and fractional routing have the same achievable rate region. We construct a counterexample refuting this conjecture and use it to reduce block transfers in external-memory data rearrangement, thereby accelerating external-memory integer sorting and answering in the affirmative the longstanding question of Aggarwal and Vitter (1988) on whether integer operations can beat the comparison-sorting input/output (I/O) bound. Specifically, we give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $\Theta(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is \[ O\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+ \frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon} \right]\right), \] where $\varepsilon=1.5\times10^{-5}$ is an absolute constant. This bound asymptotically improves on the classical $\Theta\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+ \frac{\log(N/M)}{\log(M/B)}\right]\right)$ comparison-sorting bound in certain parameter regimes. Under the external-memory model specified in this paper, we have formally verified the algorithm's correctness and I/O complexity bound in Lean~4.

papers.title: Leveraging Recourse and Size Bounds for OnlineKnapsack with Removable Items
papers.abstract: In the online unweighted knapsack problem, items arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected immediately for a bounded-capacity knapsack, aiming to maximize the total size of accepted items. When decisions are irrevocable, no algorithm achieves a non-trivial competitive ratio. An essential relaxation that circumvents this impossibility is to allow previously accepted items to be removed from the knapsack (a.k.a. removal). In this work, we investigate possible further improvements on the competitive ratio with removal by bringing together two other previously proposed model extensions: knowledge of an upper bound on the item sizes (a.k.a. bound awareness) and ability to reinsert previously rejected items(a.k.a.recourse). Our contributions are twofold. First, we establish close upper and lower bounds on the competitive ratio under bound awareness, removal and recourse. We show that significant improvements on the best known competitive ratio are possible when the upper bound on the item sizes is not too restrictive and only few uses of recourse are available. Second, we introduce the notion of adaptive online algorithms which do not require to know any upper bound on the item sizes but still achieve performance guarantees comparable to the ones obtained under the bound awareness model.

papers.title: Combinatorial Algorithms for Partial Inverse Min-Max Spanning Tree Problem under the Weighted Sum Hamming Distance
papers.abstract: Given a connected weighted graph G=(V, E, w) and a forest F of G, the goal of partial inverse min-max spanning tree problem is to change the weight function as little as possible, so that there is a min-max spanning tree with respect to the new weight function containing F. In this paper, we study this problem under the weighted sum Hamming distance. We take the alternative set of the maximum edge weight in F with respect to the optimal weight function as a key factor, and further consider the case of this problem under the restriction of this factor. On this basis, a polynomial time algorithm with time complexity O(|V|^4) is proposed to solve this problem.

papers.title: FastHeapDict: Permanent Slot Indexing for Efficient Decrease-Key Operations in Indexed Priority Queues
papers.abstract: Efficient decrease-key support remains an important practical concern in priority queues used by shortest-path and graph-processing algorithms. Although duplicate-entry heaps avoid explicit decrease-key operations and are simple to implement, they may accumulate many stale entries when tentative priorities are repeatedly improved. This paper presents FastHeapDict, an indexed binary min-heap based on permanent slot indexing. Instead of repeatedly locating keys through hash-table lookups during heap repair, FastHeapDict assigns each key a stable integer slot and stores that slot directly in heap entries. As a result, position updates during sift-up and sift-down operations are performed through integer indexing while preserving the usual indexed-heap interface. We evaluate FastHeapDict in both Python and C++20 using Dijkstra's algorithm as the primary experimental workload. The benchmarks include constructed dense stress graphs, randomized dense graph variants, and comparisons against duplicate-entry heaps and existing priority-queue alternatives. Across the tested Python workloads, FastHeapDict consistently outperforms the duplicate-entry heapq baseline and the tested heapdict and pqdict implementations. In the C++20 implementation, FastHeapDict also achieves strong constant-factor improvements over std::priority_queue duplicates, std::set-based decrease-key, and std::multiset duplicates. These results indicate that permanent slot indexing can provide a compact and effective implementation strategy for indexed priority queues in workloads where priority updates are frequent.

papers.title: Online carpooling against an oblivious adversary
papers.abstract: In the online carpooling problem, edges on $n$ vertices arrive one at a time and must be oriented immediately, so as to keep the difference between the indegree and the outdegree of every vertex small. We give a randomized online algorithm which bounds the largest absolute difference over the first $T$ edges by $O((\log T)^{1/3})$ with high probability on every input sequence fixed in advance. This proves a conjecture of Kulkarni, Reis and Rothvoss and matches the known worst case lower bound. The algorithm keeps the law of the discrepancy vector dominated in the convex order by a Gaussian measure, and forces the endpoint with the smaller discrepancy to receive the edge whenever the two discrepancies are far apart. In the analysis we show that a vertex of discrepancy $D$ is preceded by a set of $O(D)$ vertices with total discrepancy $\Omega(D^2)$.

papers.title: Max Weight Independent Set in graphs with no long claws nor large induced bicliques
papers.abstract: The complexity of Max Weight Independent Set (MWIS) in graphs excluding a fixed subdivided claw is one of the central open problems in algorithmic graph theory. We show that MWIS can be solved in polynomial time in graphs excluding a fixed subdivided claw and a fixed biclique as an induced subgraph. This strengthens a result of Abrishami, Chudnovsky, Dibek, Pilipczuk, and Rz\k{a}\.zewski [ACM TALG 2026] who showed an analogous result, but under a stronger assumption that some biclique is excluded as a subgraph.

papers.title: $k$-Center under Weak and Strong Distance Oracles with an Application to Minimum Sum of Radii Clustering
papers.abstract: In the weak-strong distance oracle model of Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram and Wang (COLT 2024), a metric $(X,d)$ on $n$ points is accessed through two oracles: a cheap weak oracle that returns each queried distance correctly with probability $1-\delta$ and permits arbitrary values on corrupted pairs, chosen by an adversary who knows the entire metric and all corrupted pairs, and an expensive strong oracle that reveals a point exactly. The goal is to cluster well while making as few strong queries as possible. Our main result is a $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation for $k$-center using $O(k\log n\log(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n))$ strong point queries, for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$. This improves both the $(14+\varepsilon)$ approximation factor and the $O(k\log^2 n\log(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n))$ query bound of Bateni et al. It also improves the query complexity of the recent $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation of Pradhan, Bhattacharya and Jaiswal (AISTATS 2026), in the variant of the model they study. Our algorithm outputs an explicitly known sketch of an otherwise unknown metric: a concrete metric on at most $k$ points that a downstream algorithm can compute with directly, with no further queries and no noise. As an application, we give a simple FPT algorithm for Minimum Sum of Radii (MSR) that returns a constant-factor solution using $2^{O(k\log k)}\cdot O(\log n\log\log n)$ strong queries. We complement the upper bound with an $\Omega(k\log(n/k))$ lower bound for $k$-center with assignment that holds for row-local algorithms. These algorithms assign two unqueried points to the same center whenever their weak distances to the strong-queried points are exactly the same. Our algorithm and those of Bateni et al. and Pradhan et al. are all row-local, so our query bound is optimal for this class up to the $O(\log\log n)$ factor.
